'''Henry Abel Dye Jr.''' (1926–1986) was an American mathematician, specializing in operator algebras and ergodic theory.<ref name=cdlib>{{cite web|author=Arveson, William|author2=Blattner, Robert|authorlink2=Robert James Blattner|author3=Takesaki, Masamichi|authorlink3=Masamichi Takesaki|title=In memoriam: Henry Abel Dye 1926–1986|year=1989|website=Californian Digital Library|url=http://content.cdlib.org/view?docId=hb4p30063r;NAAN=13030&doc.view=frames&chunk.id=div00015&toc.depth=1&toc.id=&brand=calisphere}}</ref><ref name=MacTutor>{{MacTutor|id=Dye|title=Henry Abel Dye}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Dye received from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute a bachelor's degree and in 1950 a Ph.D. from the University of Chicago. As a postdoc he was from 1950 to 1952 at California Institute of Technology (Caltech) and from 1952 to 1953 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. He was from 1953 to 1956 an assistant professor at the University of Iowa, from 1956 to 1959 an associate professor at the University of Southern California (USC), and from 1959 to 1960 a full professor at the University of Iowa. From 1960 until his death in 1986 he was a full professor at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).<ref name=MacTutor/>

{{blockquote|His first published paper, "The Radon-Nikodym theorem for finite rings of operators", contained important results which led to many advances in the theory of [[von Neumann algebra]]s, for example, the non-commutative integration theory of I.E. Segal and [[Jacques Dixmier|J. Dixmier]] and the modular theory of von Neumann algebras. In other papers concerning operator algebras, he showed that the unitary group and the projection lattice of a von Neumann factor each completely determine the algebraic structure of that factor.<ref name=cdlib/>}}

{{blockquote|One of the most striking early results of [[Francis Joseph Murray|Murray]] and [[John von Neumann|von Neumann]] implied that all finite measure preserving actions of countable abelian groups give rise to isomorphic operator algebras. It was Henry Dye who discovered that this isomorphism had a more fundamental and geometric origin, and was actually induced by an isomorphism of the underlying measure spaces that carried orbits to orbits.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Varadarajan, V. S.|authorlink=Veeravalli S. Varadarajan|title=Henry Abel Dye|journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics|volume=137|issue=1|date=January 1989|pages=iii–v|url=https://msp.org/pjm/1989/137-1/pjm-v137-n1-p01-s.pdf|doi=10.2140/pjm.1989.137.iii|doi-access=free}} (quote from p. iv)</ref>}}
